subtype: Wrinkled nose at smells and tastes [Expressing]
passage: At the family's tea stall in the village, Shreya's mother Nazia lifted a spoon of methi sabzi to the toddler's lips. Shreya's nose wrinkled up and she pressed her lips shut, head pulled back. “Not yet, then,” said Nazia, and set the spoon down without fuss. Shreya ate her roti and dal instead. Two days later Nazia put a tiny bit of the sabzi beside the dal. Shreya sniffed it, wrinkled her nose again, but licked a corner and looked at her mother.

qa.q: What did Nazia offer Shreya at the tea stall?
qa.a: A spoonful of methi sabzi.

qa.q: What does Shreya's wrinkled nose suggest she felt, and what else might it mean?
qa.a: She probably felt put off, even a little disgusted, by the smell or strange taste, since she pulled her head back too. She might also simply not have been hungry for something new.

qa.q: How did Nazia handle the refusal, and what could she try next?
qa.a: She did not force it and offered it again later in a tiny amount. Next she could let Shreya see her eating it happily.

qa.q: What might Shreya feel when her mother lets it go?
qa.a: She may feel that her signal was heard, which lets her feel safe enough to try a lick another day. 🙂

grounding: A toddler wrinkles her nose at an unfamiliar food, and the adult respects the reaction and tries again later.

subtype: Wrinkled nose at smells and tastes [Expressing]
passage: Chen opened the fridge and Javier, two, standing at his knee in a Vancouver kitchen, suddenly wrinkled his whole nose and turned his face away. “Blue cheese,” said Chen, and laughed. “Strong smell, huh?” Javier waved a hand in front of his face. Chen closed the fridge door, took a slice of plain cheese instead and cut it into little pieces. Javier ate one, then another. The blue cheese stayed at the back of the shelf.

qa.q: What did Javier react to when Chen opened the fridge?
qa.a: The strong smell of the blue cheese.

qa.q: What did Javier's wrinkled nose and waving hand show he felt?
qa.a: They show dislike of the strong smell. It could also mean he was startled by the sudden odour, not that he disliked cheese in general.

qa.q: What did Chen do that respected Javier's reaction?
qa.a: He shut the fridge and offered a milder cheese instead of asking Javier to try the smelly one.

qa.q: How might Javier see Chen's laughter?
qa.a: He may see it as friendly, a sign that the smell is a normal thing to notice and that his reaction was understood. 🙂

grounding: A toddler wrinkles his nose at a bad smell, and the adult respects it without forcing food.

subtype: Wrinkled nose at smells and tastes [Expressing]
passage: I'm Deepak, Lakshmi's uncle, and I carried her through the fish market in Kochi on Saturday. The moment we passed the dried-fish stall, her whole nose crinkled up and her top lip lifted. She turned her face into my shirt. Her Amma laughed and said, "Too strong, na?" and walked us to the fruit side. I couldn't tell if she hated the smell or was just startled by it. Near the bananas she looked up again.

qa.q: Which stall made Lakshmi crinkle her nose?
qa.a: The dried-fish stall.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi's wrinkled nose and lifted lip suggest she felt?
qa.a: Most likely disgust at the strong smell; turning into Deepak's shirt might also mean she was startled or overwhelmed.

qa.q: What did Amma do that respected Lakshmi's reaction?
qa.a: She named it ("Too strong, na?") and moved them to the fruit side, without making Lakshmi stay near the smell.

qa.q: How does Deepak see the moment?
qa.a: Deepak notices the reaction clearly but isn't sure whether it was dislike or surprise.

grounding: An uncle sees a toddler wrinkle her nose at a strong market smell and her mother respects it.

subtype: Wrinkled nose at smells and tastes [Expressing]
passage:
Day one: Omkar offered Anirban a spoon of spinach dal. Anirban wrinkled his nose and pushed the spoon away. Omkar put the bowl aside and gave him rice.
Day five: a little spinach sat next to the rice on the plate. Anirban poked it, sniffed his finger, and his nose crinkled only a bit.
Day twelve: he took two bites of the green rice himself. "Okay," he announced.

qa.q: What did Omkar give Anirban on day one after he pushed the spoon away?
qa.a: He put the bowl aside and gave him rice.

qa.q: What did Anirban's wrinkled nose on day one suggest?
qa.a: Dislike or mild disgust at the new taste or smell; the smaller crinkle on day five suggests he was growing curious and less wary.

qa.q: Which approach worked, and why?
qa.a: Not forcing the dal and offering a little spinach again later worked, because Anirban could explore it at his own pace.

qa.q: What would change if Omkar had pushed the spoon into his mouth on day one?
qa.a: Anirban might have felt upset and struggled, and could have refused spinach for much longer.

grounding: Over several days a father respects his toddler's wrinkled nose at new food, offers it again later, and the child tries it.

subtype: Wrinkled nose at smells and tastes [Expressing]
passage:
The garbage van rumbled into the Delhi colony lane just as Baljeet was toddling out with his father. Baljeet stopped, screwed up his nose and squeezed his mouth tight. He pulled at his father's hand, backwards.
Yusuf, who lived on the ground floor, was watering his plants. He wrinkled his own nose and laughed. "Same, beta. Very smelly!"
Baljeet stared at him, then wrinkled his nose again, and this time he giggled.

qa.q: Who was watering plants in the lane?
qa.a: Yusuf, who lived on the ground floor.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet pull his father's hand backwards?
qa.a: He felt disgusted by the smell of the garbage van and wanted to get away from it; his giggle later suggests the shared joke made him feel better.

qa.q: How did Yusuf help turn the moment around?
qa.a: He copied the wrinkled nose and named the smell kindly, so Baljeet felt understood and could laugh.

qa.q: How might Baljeet's father see his son's reaction?
qa.a: He likely understands it as a simple reaction to a bad smell and is glad the neighbour made it light.

grounding: A toddler wrinkles his nose at a bad smell, and a neighbour accepts it and shares it playfully.

subtype: Wrinkled nose at smells and tastes [Expressing]
passage:
“Here, Chinmay, try a little karela,” said Disha, holding out the spoon.
Chinmay sniffed it. His nose wrinkled up, his top lip lifted, and he turned his head away.
“Arre, he must eat it,” said Aaji. “It's good for him.”
“He doesn't like the smell today, Aaji,” said Disha. “Look at his nose.”
“So you'll let him refuse?”
“I'll put a tiny bit on his plate again next week. No forcing.”
Chinmay grabbed a piece of chapati and smiled.

qa.q: What did Disha hold out to Chinmay on the spoon?
qa.a: She held out a little karela on the spoon.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling when his nose wrinkled up?
qa.a: He felt a quick dislike or disgust at the bitter smell, a near-reflex reaction rather than naughtiness.

qa.q: Which choice worked here, and why?
qa.a: Disha respected his dislike without forcing and planned to offer a tiny bit again later, which keeps meals calm and leaves room to try again.

qa.q: How does Aaji see Chinmay turning away?
qa.a: Aaji sees it as refusing something good for him that he should be made to eat.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler wrinkling his nose at an unfamiliar food, a reflex-like sign of dislike, and an adult not forcing it.
